summary: Describes how SSH can use the GSS-API for authentication and key exchange. It defines a user authentication method that uses a chosen GSS-API mechanism, and key exchange methods that use GSS-API to authenticate a Diffie-Hellman exchange. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4462 lets SSH use a GSS-API mechanism for key exchange and user authentication. It defines message exchanges that let the client and server establish a protected session and identify the user.

what is the ssh null host key algorithm
how does gssapi authentication work with ssh
subtitle: Adds GSS-API methods for SSH key exchange and user authentication.

tldr.problem: SSH deployments that already use a GSS-API security mechanism need a way to use it for SSH host authentication, key exchange and user authentication.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC combines GSS-API mutual authentication with Diffie-Hellman, defines gssapi-with-mic and gssapi-keyex user authentication, and adds a null host-key algorithm.
tldr.outcome: The methods can use GSS-API mechanisms such as Kerberos. RFC 4462 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8732 and RFC 9142.

today: RFC 4462 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2006. It has been updated by RFC 8732 and RFC 9142, and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Using GSS-API with SSH
sections.content:
The Generic Security Service API (GSS-API) gives applications security services without tying them to one mechanism. RFC 4462 defines SSH methods that use GSS-API for a Diffie-Hellman key exchange and for user authentication.

The specification defines a family of key exchange method names, two user authentication methods, and a null host-key algorithm. It assumes that readers know the SSH architecture, transport and user authentication specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: SSH can use a GSS-API security mechanism instead of relying only on SSH-specific credentials. This RFC defines how the SSH messages carry that exchange.

sections.title: GSS-API-Authenticated Key Exchange
sections.content:
The client and server combine Diffie-Hellman key exchange with mutual authentication through GSS-API. The client requests mutual authentication and per-message integrity. If the mechanism cannot provide either, the key exchange MUST fail.

After exchanging GSS-API tokens, the server and client calculate a shared secret and an exchange hash from the SSH version strings, key-exchange messages, public values and shared secret. The server sends a message integrity code (MIC) for the hash, and the client verifies it. The method does not require a public-key signature or encryption operation for the key exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server establish a shared secret while GSS-API authenticates the exchange. They verify a message integrity code before accepting the key exchange.

sections.title: Selecting a Group and Method
sections.content:
The group-exchange variant lets the client send minimum, preferred and maximum Diffie-Hellman group sizes. The server selects a suitable safe prime and generator. Implementations SHOULD support group sizes from 1024 to 8192 bits.

Each key-exchange method name combines a fixed prefix with a value derived from the underlying GSS-API mechanism's object identifier. The prefixes defined here include gss-group1-sha1-, gss-group14-sha1- and gss-gex-sha1-. Names beginning with gss- are reserved for conforming methods.
sections.plainLanguage: The client can request acceptable group sizes, and the server chooses a group within that request. The method name identifies which GSS-API mechanism and key-exchange method the peers selected.

sections.title: The gssapi-with-mic Method
sections.content:
For gssapi-with-mic, the client sends the GSS-API mechanism identifiers it supports in preference order. The server selects the first one it supports, and the peers exchange GSS-API tokens until authentication succeeds or fails.

When the mechanism supports per-message integrity, the client sends a MIC over the SSH session identifier and authentication request. This binds the authentication to the session. A server MUST NOT accept a request for a user that does not exist, though it may avoid revealing that fact by disconnecting or returning a misleading list of methods.
sections.plainLanguage: The client lists its supported mechanisms, and the server selects one before they exchange authentication tokens. A MIC can bind the result to this SSH session so it cannot simply be replayed in another session.

sections.title: Reusing Key-Exchange Authentication
sections.content:
The gssapi-keyex method uses the GSS-API context established during the initial key exchange to authenticate a user. It sends one request containing a MIC over the session identifier and request fields. It can be used only when the initial key exchange used a conforming GSS-API method; a context created during rekeying MUST NOT be used.

The null host-key algorithm has no host-key material and provides neither signature nor encryption. It is intended for configurations where the key exchange is authenticated by another mechanism. A server MUST NOT advertise it unless it is the only host-key algorithm advertised.
sections.plainLanguage: A user-authentication method can refer to the GSS-API context already established during the first key exchange. The null host-key option applies only when another mechanism authenticates that exchange.

sections.title: Naming and Security Requirements
sections.content:
The client identifies the server to GSS-API with a host-based service name built from the server's hostname. Implementations MUST NOT use insecure DNS results to construct this name. A client that cannot determine the name securely SHOULD NOT use the mechanism.

Key exchange depends on the GSS-API mechanism providing mutual authentication and per-message integrity. If either is unavailable, the exchange MUST fail. The RFC also prohibits SPNEGO as the underlying mechanism because it can interfere with SSH's own method negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The client must identify the server securely. Key exchange fails if the GSS-API mechanism cannot authenticate both sides and protect the exchange's integrity.
